newsitem.title: UK: UK parties scrap over trust, poll gap narrows.
newsitem.headline: UK parties scrap over trust, poll gap narrows.

text.p: On the fifth anniversary of the Conservatives' last victory at the polls, Britain's two main political parties bickered on Wednesday over which deserved voters' trust at the May 1 general election.

Opinion polls showing that Labour's lead over the ruling Conservatives was narrowing boosted Prime Minister John Major, who said his Labour rival Tony Blair had already turned key areas of policy "on their head" in the campaign.

"His manifesto is falling apart under the pressure of the general election. Saying one thing one day and another thing the next is no basis either for trust, or for any belief in his competence," Major told a news conference.
Blair hit back, accusing Major of repeatedly failing to honour promises he made to the electorate at the 1992 election, notably by raising taxes after pledging to cut them.

"Their record in government robs their manifesto of any shred of credibility. After five years of betrayal and broken promises, they no longer deserve the people's trust. They have become unfit to rule," Blair said.
The clash came after a Guardian newspaper opinion poll showed the lowest Labour lead of the campaign -- 12 points.

A Daily Telegraph poll also showed a narrowing gap -- 19 points, from 26 on March 26. One taken in Scotland put Labour support there down two points to 51 percent. Major pulled off a surprise win in 1992 after being behind in pre-election polls.
Even the Guardian poll points to a huge Labour majority of 109 seats in the next parliament, but Conservative strategists hope the inexperienced Blair will falter at the final hurdle.

They say they see the first signs of this in a flurry of Labour policy adjustments in recent days following Conservative claims that Labour's manifesto pledges would inevitably mean either higher taxes or rocketing government borrowing.

Labour is now refusing to rule out privatisation of Britain's air traffic control system, a Conservative plan denounced just a few months ago as irresponsible by Labour transport spokesman Andrew Smith.
Major said that in launching the Labour manifesto last week, Blair had said nothing about privatisation, a policy which even his centrist "New Labour" party has traditionally opposed.

"A few days later he said something different. And so it goes on -- a different policy every day. For years he has been saying different things to different audiences. Now he's finally been caught out," Major said.
But Blair said Major had betrayed Britons' trust in him in the five years since he won the April 9, 1992 election.

Flourishing the Conservative 1992 manifesto, he declared: "If I had stood on this platform five years ago and made the promises Mr Major made...I would not have the gall to ask the British people to trust me again."
The spat between the two parties on trust was welcome relief for the Conservatives, who have spent much of the campaign having to deal with allegations of "sleaze" against MPs.

Neil Hamilton, a former minister accused of accepting wads of 50 pound ($80) notes in brown envelopes for asking parliamentary questions on behalf of Harrods store owner Mohamed Al-Fayed, was on Tuesday readopted as a Conservative candidate.

Hamilton, who maintains his innocence, faces a challenge in the north-west England seat of Tatton from BBC reporter Martin Bell. The war correspondent announced on Sunday he would stand as an anti-corruption independent with the backing of Labour and the minority Liberal Democrats.
Asked what he would do as a Tatton elector, Major said: "I would vote for Neil Hamilton."
